body_html:
English words that don’t translate to Spanish neatly are part of my daily work as a translator. Some English words have no single Spanish equivalent; others have one dictionary translation that natives rarely use in that context. Words like “awkward”, “nice” and “cozy” look simple, yet each needs a different Spanish word depending on the situation. Here’s my list of the trickiest ones, with the natural Spanish you can use instead. (For the reverse direction, see {{link:spanish-words-with-no-english-translation|Spanish words with no English translation}}.)

Key takeaways
  • Many everyday English words split into several Spanish words depending on context.
  • Translate the situation, not the word.
  • Some English words are borrowed directly in Spanish (el brunch, el fin de semana), but many are not.
  • When in doubt, describe: Spanish is comfortable using a phrase where English uses one word.
{{toc}}

English words that don’t translate to Spanish: the classics

EnglishNatural Spanish (by context)
awkwardincómodo (situation), torpe (clumsy person), violento (Spain, embarrassing moment), un silencio incómodo
nicesimpático, buena onda (person), bonito (thing), rico (food), agradable (weather, evening)
cozyacogedor (place), calentito, a gusto: Estoy muy a gusto aquí.
overwhelmedagobiado, abrumado, desbordado
cheesycursi (romantic), hortera (Spain, tacky)
commuteel trayecto al trabajo, ir y venir del trabajo
siblingshermanos (covers brothers and sisters)
toddlerniño pequeño, niño de dos años

The Fundéu RAE regularly suggests Spanish alternatives for English words that are creeping into Spanish.

Feelings that need a phrase

  • to be excited about: tener ganas de, hacer ilusión: Me hace mucha ilusión el viaje. (Not excitado; see {{link:embarrassing-spanish-mistakes|embarrassing Spanish mistakes}}.)
  • to be into something: estar metido en, ser muy de: Soy muy de series.
  • to have a crush on: estar colado por (Spain), gustarle mucho alguien.
  • wholesome: sano, entrañable, tierno, depending on whether it’s food, a story or a person.
  • to feel homesick: echar de menos mi casa, tener morriña (Galicia), extrañar.

More emotion vocabulary in {{link:talking-about-feelings-in-spanish|talking about feelings in Spanish}}.

{{image:2}}

Little words that do a lot

Get

English “get” has no single equivalent. Conseguir (get = obtain), llegar (get home), ponerse (get nervous), entender (I get it), recibir (get a message). See {{link:ponerse-volverse-hacerse|ponerse, volverse and hacerse}}.

Mind

“Do you mind?” is ¿Te importa?; “Never mind” is No importa or Da igual; “mind your head” is cuidado con la cabeza; “in my mind” is en mi cabeza.

Random

Mathematical “random” is aleatorio, but casual “random” is cualquiera (a random guy: un tipo cualquiera), raro (that was random: qué raro) or al azar (at random).

Fun

The adjective is divertido, but “to have fun” is pasarlo bien or divertirse, and “for fun” is por diversión or por gusto.

{{book:the-mind-lies}}

Words Spanish has borrowed

Some English words are used directly in Spanish, especially in Spain and in tech: el wifi, el brunch, el spoiler, el selfi (adapted spelling), hacer footing (Spain, jogging). Others have local versions: el correo electrónico (email), la contraseña (password), la computadora (Latin America) / el ordenador (Spain).

How I handle these words as a translator

When I meet a word like “awkward” in an English text, I never look for the translation. I ask what it is doing in that sentence: describing a silence, a person, a design, a moment? Then I choose the Spanish word a native writer would use in that same scene. Sometimes that’s one word, sometimes a short phrase, and occasionally the sentence needs restructuring. This is also the best approach for learners: build a small list of context-specific options rather than a single equivalent.

A few more worth knowing

  • privacy: privacidad (data, settings) but intimidad (personal life): Respeta mi intimidad.
  • to binge-watch: ver una serie de un tirón, darse un atracón de series.
  • pet peeve: algo que me saca de quicio, una manía.
  • to make it (succeed or arrive): lograrlo, llegar a tiempo, triunfar.

Each one shows the same principle: Spanish often prefers a short, vivid phrase to a single borrowed word.

Common mistakes

LiteralNatural
Es una persona muy bonita. (nice)Es una persona muy simpática / muy buena onda.
Estoy excitado por el viaje.Me hace mucha ilusión el viaje.
¿Lo consigues? (Do you get it?)¿Lo entiendes?
un tipo aleatorio (a random guy)un tipo cualquiera
Tuvimos mucha diversión.Lo pasamos muy bien.
{{image:3}}

Try it yourself

  1. It was an awkward silence. (Fue un silencio incómodo.)
  2. This café is so cozy. (Esta cafetería es muy acogedora.)
  3. I’m overwhelmed with work. (Estoy agobiado de trabajo.)
  4. Never mind. (No importa. / Da igual.)
  5. We had so much fun. (Lo pasamos genial.)

Related: {{link:literal-translation-mistakes-spanish|literal translation mistakes in Spanish}} and {{link:common-spanish-mistakes|my guide to common Spanish mistakes}}.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

When an English word has no Spanish twin, don’t force one. Look at the situation, choose the word a native would use there, and keep a few options for each tricky word. That habit is what turns translated Spanish into natural Spanish.

faq.q: What are some English words that don’t translate to Spanish?
faq.a: Awkward, nice, cozy, overwhelmed, cheesy, commute, get, mind and random have no single Spanish equivalent; the right word depends on context.

faq.q: How do you say “awkward” in Spanish?
faq.a: Incómodo for situations (un silencio incómodo), torpe for clumsy people and violento in Spain for embarrassing moments.

faq.q: How do you say “I’m excited” in Spanish?
faq.a: Tengo muchas ganas or Me hace mucha ilusión. Avoid excitado, which has a sexual meaning.
